## 2

I can see why you'd be suspicious of photos, since images can be edited. But you don't need space photos to check the shape of the Earth. People worked it out over 2,000 years ago with simple observations you can repeat yourself:

- **Ships at sea:** A ship sailing away disappears from the bottom up, hull first and mast last. On a flat surface it would just shrink until it was too small to see.
- **Lunar eclipses:** The Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round, whatever angle the eclipse happens at. Only a sphere casts a round shadow from every direction.
- **Different stars:** Travel far enough north or south and you see different constellations. In Australia you can't see Polaris at all.
- **Time zones:** When it's noon in London, it's night in Sydney. A single sun over a flat disc can't light one part and leave another in darkness like that.
- **Measuring it:** Around 240 BC, Eratosthenes compared shadow angles in two Egyptian cities on the same day and estimated the Earth's circumference fairly accurately.

What would count as convincing evidence for you? If there's a test you'd trust, I'm happy to work through it together.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colours of the rainbow mixed together. You can see this when light passes through a prism or makes a rainbow.

Each colour of light is a wave, and the colours have different wavelengths. Red light has long, lazy waves. Blue light has short, choppy ones.

When sunlight comes into the atmosphere, it hits the tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen that make up air. These molecules are much smaller than the light waves, and they bounce short waves around far more than long ones. Blue light gets scattered about five or six times as much as red. So blue light ends up bouncing all over the sky and reaching your eyes from every direction, while most of the red, orange and yellow light travels straight through. Look anywhere away from the Sun and you see that scattered blue.

You might ask: violet has even shorter waves, so why isn't the sky violet? The Sun gives off less violet than blue, some violet gets absorbed high in the atmosphere, and your eyes are much more sensitive to blue. The mix your eyes receive looks sky blue.

The same idea explains sunsets. When the Sun is low, its light passes through much more air to reach you. By then most of the blue has been scattered away, and what's left is the reds and oranges.
